text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rose from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. It was the third lunar landing attempt, and by then the public had begun to treat such flights as routine. Jim Lovell, the commander, was the most experienced astronaut alive, a veteran of three spaceflights who had already circled the Moon once. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was a rookie on his first mission. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original command module pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons. Swigert stepped in after a hurried round of training.

The first two days passed quietly. The crew named their command module Odyssey and their lunar module Aquarius. They coasted outward, ran television broadcasts that few networks bothered to carry, and joked with Mission Control in Houston. Then, on the night of April 13, about fifty-five hours into the flight and roughly 200,000 miles from home, Houston asked Swigert to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module. The tanks held supercooled liquid that tended to settle, and a stir kept the gauges accurate.

Swigert flipped the switch. A little over a minute later, the crew heard a loud bang, and the spacecraft shuddered. Warning lights came on. Swigert reported a problem, and Lovell repeated it in the line that became famous: "Houston, we've had a problem."

At first nobody understood how bad it was. Voltage readings dropped, and a thruster fired by itself. Then Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming into space. Oxygen tank number two had ruptured and damaged tank number one, and the three fuel cells that made the ship's electricity and water depended on that oxygen. Within about two hours, the command module was dying. The Moon landing was over. The question now was whether the crew could survive at all.

The investigation that followed traced the cause to a chain of small errors. Years earlier, the tank had been dropped slightly during handling. Later, during a ground test, the tank would not drain properly, and technicians ran its heaters at a high voltage to boil off the oxygen. That overheated the wiring and damaged its Teflon insulation, though no one recognized it. When Swigert hit the switch, a spark in the exposed wiring ignited the insulation in the pure oxygen, the pressure spiked, and the tank burst.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz and his teams of controllers went to work. The plan that saved the crew was to treat the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius had its own power, oxygen, and water, but it was built to support two men for about two days on the Moon, not three men for four days in deep space. Lovell and Haise moved into it, and Swigert shut down Odyssey to save its remaining battery power for the return to Earth's atmosphere.

Next came the trajectory. The ship had been on a path that would carry it around the Moon and back toward Earth, but the course had been adjusted to aim for a landing site, so it would not have returned the crew safely without more help. Controllers chose to fire the lunar module's descent engine to speed the trip home. After swinging around the far side of the Moon, the crew fired the engine a second time to shorten the journey to about two days. Lovell, Haise, and Swigert had become the farthest humans from Earth in history, nearly 250,000 miles away, though they had little time to appreciate it.

Then came the problem of air. The lunar module's lithium hydroxide canisters, which scrubbed exhaled carbon dioxide, were filling up, and the spare canisters from the command module were square while the lunar module's sockets were round. Carbon dioxide levels crept toward dangerous territory. On the ground, engineers gathered the same materials the crew had on board, such as plastic bags, cardboard, suit hoses, and duct tape, and worked out a way to join a square canister to a round socket. They read the instructions to the crew step by step, and the crew built the adapter. The readings fell.

Life aboard the cramped little ship was miserable. To save power, almost everything was switched off, and the temperature fell to near freezing. Condensation beaded on the walls. The men slept little and drank little, because water was needed to cool the electronics, and each of them was limited to a few ounces a day. Haise developed a fever and a painful infection, and Lovell later estimated that the three men lost a combined total of around thirty pounds. They wore their flight suits and, at times, snug overshoes, and sat shivering while the lunar module carried them home.

Meanwhile, Mattingly, the astronaut who had been bumped from the crew, worked in a simulator in Houston with other engineers to design a way to restart Odyssey using as little power as possible. A normal start up took hours and drew far more energy than was left. The team wrote a new procedure, tested it, and read it up to the crew. They also had to solve a navigation problem. The ship's guidance system had been shut down, so the crew had to line up their position by hand, using the Sun and the Earth's edge as references. A small engine burn on the way back corrected the angle, because an error in the entry path of even a degree or two could skip the capsule off the atmosphere or burn it up.

Shortly before reentry, the crew discarded the damaged service module. As it drifted away, they saw for the first time what the explosion had done. A whole panel was gone, and the side of the module was torn open and trailing debris. Lovell reported it to Houston, and the scale of the damage made clear how lucky they were to be alive. They then climbed back into Odyssey, said goodbye to Aquarius, and let the lunar module go. It would burn up over the Pacific.

On April 17, the command module hit the atmosphere. The heat shield had to work perfectly, and nobody could be sure that it had survived the explosion. During every reentry, radio contact is lost for several minutes while the ionized air around the capsule blocks signals. This time the blackout stretched longer than expected, and in Houston, the controllers sat silent, watching the clock. Then the parachutes opened, and Swigert's voice came through. Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific near Samoa, within sight of the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The mission had lasted almost 143 hours.

Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, yet it is often called a successful failure. The crew survived because of the lunar module, but also because of the improvisation of hundreds of people on the ground, who had to find solutions to problems no one had planned for. A review board examined the tank's design and the handling that had weakened it. NASA changed the design of the oxygen tanks and the way they were tested and handled, and Apollo missions resumed with a safer spacecraft. For the public, the flight became a story about calm, teamwork, and skill under pressure, and about how three men in a freezing ship got home.
